definition: To have enough money or time to pay for or do something.
examples: I can't afford a new phone this month.
Can we afford to hire another person before December?

pattern.rule: afford + noun / to + verb (usually with can/could)

cloze.sentence: Rent in Lagos is so high that many students can't ___ their own flat.

formDrill.sentence: Is the new laptop ___ for most students?

fix.wrong: I can't afford buying a car.
fix.right: I can't afford to buy a car.
fix.why: After 'afford' use to + verb, not -ing.

distractors: To refuse to pay for something.
To borrow money from a bank.
To be happy with the price of something.
tip: Afford is almost always used with can, could or be able to, not in simple tenses like 'I afford it'.

definition: Possible to do and likely to work in practice.
examples: The engineers say the plan is feasible if we get more funding.
It isn't feasible to finish the whole project in one week.

pattern.rule: feasible + noun / it is feasible + to + verb
pattern.example: It is feasible to deliver by Friday.

cloze.sentence: The plan looked good on paper, but was it really ___ with only half the budget?

formDrill.sentence: We checked the ___ of the idea before spending any money.

fix.wrong: The project is feasibly, so we can start.
fix.right: The project is feasible, so we can start.
fix.why: After 'is', use the adjective 'feasible', not the adverb.

distractors: Very expensive and difficult to buy.
tip: Feasible is about whether something can be done; 'possible' is more general and less formal.

definition: Dealing with problems in a sensible, practical way instead of following ideas or theories.
examples: Our manager is pragmatic: she picks the solution that works fastest.
Be pragmatic and accept the smaller offer for now.

cloze.sentence: Instead of arguing about the perfect plan, the CEO took a ___ approach and fixed the problem.

formDrill.sentence: She solves problems ___, without fuss or theory.

fix.wrong: He is pragmatic in money, so he saves every month.
fix.right: He is pragmatic about money, so he saves every month.
fix.why: Use 'pragmatic about' for the subject you are practical on.

distractors: Always following strict rules and tradition.
Interested only in art and beauty.
tip: Pragmatic is usually positive; it means practical, not 'ruthless'.

definition: Having more than one possible meaning, so it is not clear what is intended.
examples: His text was ambiguous, so I didn't know if he was coming.
The contract has an ambiguous clause about payment dates.

pattern.rule: ambiguous + noun / it is ambiguous whether...

cloze.sentence: The email was so ___ that three people understood it three different ways.

formDrill.sentence: There is a lot of ___ in the job description, so ask questions.

fix.wrong: The message was ambiguity, so I asked him to explain.
fix.right: The message was ambiguous, so I asked him to explain.
fix.why: Use the adjective 'ambiguous' to describe a message.

distractors: Very short and to the point.
tip: Don't confuse ambiguous (unclear meaning) with ambitious (wanting success).

definition: Logical and well organized, so that the parts fit together and are easy to follow.
examples: She gave a coherent explanation of why sales dropped.
His essay wasn't coherent; the ideas jumped around.

cloze.sentence: After the accident he was too shocked to give a ___ account of what happened.

formDrill.sentence: Try to explain your ideas ___ so the audience can follow them.

fix.wrong: Your essay is not coherence; the paragraphs don't connect.
fix.right: Your essay is not coherent; the paragraphs don't connect.
fix.why: After 'is' use the adjective 'coherent', not the noun.

distractors: Very strong and hard to break.
Willing to work together in a team.
tip: The opposite is 'incoherent', often used for speech that makes no sense.

definition: Able to recover quickly after difficulty, loss or change.
examples: Small businesses in the city proved resilient during the fuel shortage.
Children are often more resilient than parents expect.

pattern.example: The crop is resilient to drought.

cloze.sentence: After losing his job twice, he stayed ___ and started his own company.

formDrill.sentence: Her ___ helped her return to work quickly after the illness.

fix.wrong: She is very resilient at stress.
fix.right: She is very resilient to stress.
fix.why: Use 'resilient to' for the thing someone survives.

distractors: Calm only when things are easy.
tip: Resilient can describe people, businesses, materials and economies.

definition: Honest and direct in what you say, even when the truth is uncomfortable.
examples: Thanks for being candid about the budget problems.
In a candid interview, the footballer admitted he was afraid.

pattern.example: He was candid about his mistakes.

cloze.sentence: Let me be ___ with you: the presentation needs a lot more work.

formDrill.sentence: To speak ___, I don't think the plan will work.

fix.wrong: He was candid on his failures.
fix.right: He was candid about his failures.
fix.why: Use 'candid about' a topic.

distractors: Dressed in a smart, formal way.
tip: Don't confuse candid with candidate (a person applying for a job).

definition: To be grateful for something, or to understand how important or difficult it is.
examples: I really appreciate you picking me up from the airport.
Customers appreciated the quick delivery.

pattern.rule: appreciate + noun / -ing (the thing, not the person)

cloze.sentence: I would ___ it if you could send the invoice by Monday.

formDrill.sentence: The staff wrote a note of ___ to the manager.

fix.wrong: I am very appreciate your help.
fix.right: I really appreciate your help.
fix.why: 'Appreciate' is a verb, so it needs no 'am/is' before it.

distractors: To make something look more attractive.
To increase the price of something quickly.
To feel sorry about a mistake.
tip: We appreciate things or actions, not people: say 'I appreciate your help', not 'I appreciate you' for help.

definition: Working carefully and steadily, putting in a lot of effort.
examples: She is a diligent student who never misses homework.
Thanks to his diligent work, the audit finished early.

pattern.example: He is diligent in checking every figure.

cloze.sentence: The ___ intern double-checked every spreadsheet before sending it.

formDrill.sentence: She studied ___ for months before the exam.

fix.wrong: He is very diligent on his work.
fix.right: He is very diligent in his work.
fix.why: Use 'diligent in' (or just 'diligent') with work.

tip: Diligent describes steady hard work, not natural intelligence.

definition: Certain to happen and impossible to avoid.
examples: With so many cars, traffic jams are inevitable in Lagos.
It was inevitable that prices would rise after the fuel increase.

pattern.rule: it is inevitable + that clause / inevitable + noun
pattern.example: It is inevitable that mistakes will happen.

cloze.sentence: Delays were ___ once the strike began.

formDrill.sentence: When a company grows quickly, mistakes will ___ happen.

fix.wrong: It is inevitable to fail sometimes.
fix.right: Failing sometimes is inevitable.
fix.why: 'Inevitable' does not take a to-infinitive; use a that clause or a different structure.

tip: Inevitable is stronger than 'likely': it means nothing can stop it.

definition: Seeming reasonable and likely to be true.
examples: Her excuse for being late sounded plausible.
Police said it was a plausible explanation for the missing money.

pattern.rule: plausible + noun / it is plausible that...
pattern.example: It is plausible that he forgot.

cloze.sentence: The story seemed ___ until we checked the dates.

formDrill.sentence: The excuse was so ___ that nobody believed it.

fix.wrong: It is plausible to believe that he is right.
fix.right: It is plausible that he is right.
fix.why: Plausible is followed by a that clause rather than to + verb.

distractors: Said in a loud and angry way.
tip: Plausible means it seems true, not that it is true.

definition: To make someone believe something is true or agree to do something.
examples: I couldn't convince my father to lend me the car.
The data convinced the board that we should expand.

pattern.rule: convince + person + to + verb / that clause / of + noun

cloze.sentence: It took two hours to ___ the landlord to lower the rent.

formDrill.sentence: Her argument was very ___, so we agreed.

fix.wrong: She convinced me for join the gym.
fix.right: She convinced me to join the gym.
fix.why: Use convince + person + to + verb.

distractors: To ask someone politely for a favor.
To hide the truth from someone.
tip: Convince is about belief or decision; 'persuade' is similar but focuses on getting someone to act.

definition: Small and delicate, not obvious, so it is easy to miss.
examples: There is a subtle difference between the two phone models.
He gave a subtle hint that it was time to go.

pattern.example: There was a subtle change in her tone.

cloze.sentence: The ___ smell of lemon in the soap was pleasant but not too strong.

formDrill.sentence: Her tone changed ___, and I knew she was upset.

fix.wrong: The difference is very subtle to notice it.
fix.right: The difference is very subtle.
fix.why: Don't add 'to notice it'; subtle already means hard to notice.

tip: The b is silent: say /ˈsʌt.əl/.

definition: Real and clear enough to be seen, touched or measured.
examples: The training produced tangible results within three months.
There was no tangible proof that he had paid.

cloze.sentence: Investors want ___ proof that the app makes money.

formDrill.sentence: A company's reputation is ___: you cannot touch it, but it affects sales.

fix.wrong: The course gave me tangibly benefits.
fix.right: The course gave me tangible benefits.
fix.why: Use the adjective 'tangible' before a noun, not the adverb.

distractors: Owned by more than one person.
tip: The opposite is 'intangible', e.g. brand reputation or goodwill.

definition: Able to do many different things or be used in many ways.
examples: Rice is a versatile food; you can cook it many ways.
He is a versatile player who can play in any position.

cloze.sentence: A good phone case should be ___ enough for work and travel.

formDrill.sentence: Employers value ___ because it lets one person handle many tasks.

fix.wrong: She is a versatility player.
fix.right: She is a versatile player.
fix.why: Use the adjective 'versatile' before a noun.

distractors: Able to do only one task well.
Very expensive but low in quality.
Quick to break or wear out.
tip: Versatile is a strong compliment for people, skills and products.

definition: To offer an idea or plan for someone to think about.
examples: I suggest we start the meeting at ten.
She suggested taking a taxi instead of the bus.

pattern.rule: suggest + -ing / that + subject + verb (not suggest + person + to)
pattern.example: I suggest going early. / I suggest that he waits.

cloze.sentence: Can anyone ___ a good restaurant near the office?

formDrill.sentence: Do you have any ___ for improving the app?

fix.wrong: He suggested me to take a break.
fix.right: He suggested that I take a break.
fix.why: After 'suggest' don't use person + to-infinitive; use a that clause or -ing.

distractors: To order someone firmly to do a task.
To describe something in full detail.
tip: 'Suggest' can also mean 'show indirectly': The results suggest that sales are falling.

definition: Able to work well or succeed, especially in business or practical terms.
examples: Is selling snacks at the school gate a viable business?
The council is looking for a viable alternative to the old road.

cloze.sentence: Without enough customers, the shop was not ___ and had to close.

formDrill.sentence: Investors questioned the ___ of the startup.

fix.wrong: The plan is viable to succeed.
fix.right: The plan is viable.
fix.why: Don't add 'to succeed'; viable already means able to succeed.

distractors: Too risky to try at all.
tip: Viable is common with 'business', 'option' and 'alternative'.

definition: To communicate a message, idea or feeling to someone.
examples: The photo conveys how crowded the market was.
I tried to convey my thanks, but the words felt small.

pattern.example: She conveyed the news to the team.

cloze.sentence: A short, clear email will ___ the main point better than a long one.

formDrill.sentence: Her smile ___ more than words could.

fix.wrong: He conveyed me the message.
fix.right: He conveyed the message to me.
fix.why: Convey needs 'to' before the person.

distractors: To carry out a plan on time.
To change a message into another language.
tip: Convey is more formal than 'tell' or 'pass on'.

definition: Able to be believed or trusted because it seems honest and sensible.
examples: A credible witness told the court what she saw.
The company needs a credible plan to repay its loans.

cloze.sentence: Check that the news comes from a ___ source before you share it.

formDrill.sentence: Missing deadlines damaged his ___ with clients.

fix.wrong: The story was so incredible that everyone trusted it.
fix.right: The story was so credible that everyone trusted it.
fix.why: 'Incredible' means hard to believe; 'credible' means believable.

tip: Credible (believable) is different from credulous (too ready to believe).

definition: Able to be trusted to work well or do what is promised.
examples: My car is old but very reliable.
Is this website a reliable source of news?

cloze.sentence: Our internet is not ___; it cuts out every afternoon.

formDrill.sentence: The bus does not run ___, so I leave early.

fix.wrong: She is very reliable person.
fix.right: She is a very reliable person.
fix.why: A singular countable noun still needs 'a' after the adjective phrase.

tip: The verb is 'rely on', with the preposition 'on'.

definition: Made up of many different types of people or things.
examples: Lagos has a diverse population from every part of Nigeria.
Our team is diverse: five countries, four languages.

cloze.sentence: The university has a ___ student body from over forty countries.

formDrill.sentence: Companies benefit from ___ in their teams.

fix.wrong: The team is very diversity.
fix.right: The team is very diverse.
fix.why: After 'is', use the adjective 'diverse', not the noun.

distractors: Exactly the same in every way.
tip: Diverse and different are related, but diverse describes a group with many kinds.

definition: Having many parts or details and carefully planned or made.
examples: They organized an elaborate wedding with five hundred guests.
The thieves had an elaborate plan to get into the bank.

cloze.sentence: He wrote an ___ excuse that took ten minutes to read.

formDrill.sentence: The room was ___ decorated with gold and lights.

fix.wrong: Could you elaborate about your idea?
fix.right: Could you elaborate on your idea?
fix.why: The verb takes 'on', meaning 'explain in more detail'.

tip: As a verb, /ɪˈlæb.ə.reɪt/, 'elaborate on' means to give more details.

definition: To give special importance to something so people notice it.
examples: The coach emphasized the importance of arriving early.
In your CV, emphasize skills that match the job.

pattern.example: She emphasized that safety comes first.

cloze.sentence: The teacher wanted to ___ how important practice is.

formDrill.sentence: The manager put great ___ on punctuality.

fix.wrong: He emphasized on the need for rest.
fix.right: He emphasized the need for rest.
fix.why: Emphasize is transitive and takes no 'on'; the noun 'emphasis' takes 'on'.

distractors: To hide a detail from others.
To make an idea simpler to follow.
tip: British spelling is emphasise; both are correct.

definition: After a long time or a lot of effort, at the end of a process.
examples: We waited two hours and eventually the bus arrived.
He eventually paid back the money.

pattern.rule: eventually + verb (before main verb or at the start)

cloze.sentence: After many failed tries, he ___ passed his driving test.

formDrill.sentence: The ___ winner was announced after three rounds.

fix.wrong: I will eventually come tomorrow.
fix.right: I will come tomorrow.
fix.why: 'Eventually' means after a long time, not a near, planned time.

tip: Eventually is NOT 'maybe' (French/Spanish false friend); it means 'in the end'.

definition: To improve the quality, value or strength of something.
examples: New lights will enhance the look of the shop.
Online courses can enhance your chances of promotion.

cloze.sentence: A little salt can ___ the flavor of the soup.

formDrill.sentence: The update brought several ___ to the app.

fix.wrong: This course will enhance my to speak English.
fix.right: This course will enhance my English.
fix.why: Enhance takes a noun object, not a to-infinitive.

distractors: To make something shorter or smaller.
tip: Enhance is for things that are already good, to make them better.

definition: Stated clearly and in detail, leaving no doubt about what is meant.
examples: The rules are explicit: no phones in the exam hall.
She gave me explicit instructions on how to open the account.

pattern.example: He was explicit about the deadline.

cloze.sentence: The manager gave ___ permission to leave early.

formDrill.sentence: The contract ___ states that payment is due in 30 days.

fix.wrong: He was explicit in the price when we spoke.
fix.right: He was explicit about the price when we spoke.
fix.why: Use 'explicit about' a topic.

distractors: Hinted at but not directly said.
Very short and easy to forget.
tip: Explicit can also describe adult content, e.g. 'explicit lyrics'.

definition: Suggested or understood without being said directly.
examples: There was an implicit warning in his smile.
We have an implicit agreement not to discuss salaries.

pattern.example: The threat was implicit in his words.

cloze.sentence: Her silence was an ___ yes to the proposal.

formDrill.sentence: I trust my brother ___ with my money.

fix.wrong: The rule is implicit on the contract.
fix.right: The rule is implicit in the contract.
fix.why: Use 'implicit in' for something contained but not stated.

tip: Implicit is the opposite of explicit; learners often swap them.

definition: In fact; used to say what is really true, often when it is surprising.
examples: I thought the exam was hard, but it was actually quite easy.
Actually, I'm not free on Friday; can we meet Monday?

pattern.rule: actually + verb / at the start of a correction

cloze.sentence: He looks young, but he is ___ forty years old.

formDrill.sentence: The ___ cost was much higher than the quote.

fix.wrong: Actually I live in Abuja, but I will move next year.
fix.right: Currently I live in Abuja, but I will move next year.
fix.why: 'Actually' means 'in fact', not 'at the present time'.

distractors: In the same way as before.
tip: Actually does not mean 'at present'; use 'currently' or 'now' for that.

definition: To help something develop and grow over time.
examples: Good teachers foster a love of reading in children.
The program aims to foster teamwork across departments.

cloze.sentence: A friendly office can ___ better teamwork.

formDrill.sentence: Careful ___ of young talent has made the club successful.

fix.wrong: The teacher fostered the students to read.
fix.right: The teacher encouraged the students to read.
fix.why: Foster takes a noun like 'a love of reading', not person + to-verb.

distractors: To buy something for a low price.
tip: Foster can also mean caring for a child who isn't yours, as in 'foster parent'.

definition: Forming the most basic and important part of something.
examples: Honesty is fundamental to any good friendship.
The report found a fundamental problem in the design.

cloze.sentence: Clean water is a ___ human right.

formDrill.sentence: The two plans differ ___ in how they use money.

fix.wrong: Trust is fundamental for teamwork.
fix.right: Trust is fundamental to teamwork.
fix.why: Use 'fundamental to'.

tip: The noun 'fundamentals' means the basic rules, e.g. 'the fundamentals of accounting'.

definition: To make it harder for someone to do something or for something to happen.
examples: Heavy rain hindered the rescue team.
A weak internet connection can hinder online learning.

cloze.sentence: Poor roads ___ the delivery of goods to rural areas.

formDrill.sentence: Fear can be a serious ___ to success.

fix.wrong: Rain hindered us to arrive.
fix.right: Rain hindered us from arriving.
fix.why: Use hinder + person + from + -ing.

distractors: To remind someone of a task.
tip: Hinder is slightly formal; in speech people often say 'slow down' or 'get in the way of'.

definition: To take something from someone and promise to give it back later.
examples: Can I borrow your charger for an hour?
She borrowed money from the bank to start a shop.

pattern.example: I borrowed a pen from Ade.

cloze.sentence: Can I ___ your umbrella until this evening?

formDrill.sentence: The bank asked every ___ to show proof of income.

fix.wrong: Can you borrow me your pen?
fix.right: Can you lend me your pen? / Can I borrow your pen?
fix.why: You borrow FROM someone; the giver lends.

distractors: To give something to someone for a short time.
To buy something on a payment plan.
To lose something and not find it.
tip: Borrow = receive; lend = give. You borrow from a person and lend to a person.

definition: To expect something and prepare for it before it happens.
examples: We anticipate a lot of traffic on Friday evening.
Good managers anticipate problems before they grow.

cloze.sentence: The shop owner didn't ___ so many customers on the first day.

formDrill.sentence: There was great ___ before the concert began.

fix.wrong: We anticipate to finish by June.
fix.right: We expect to finish by June. / We anticipate finishing by June.
fix.why: Anticipate is followed by -ing or a noun, not to + verb.

distractors: To remember a date or name.
tip: Anticipate is stronger than 'expect': it includes getting ready.

definition: To make pain, a problem or a difficulty less severe.
examples: Painkillers alleviate the pain, but they don't cure it.
New buses should alleviate traffic on the main road.

cloze.sentence: Cash transfers can help ___ hunger in poor families.

formDrill.sentence: The ___ of poverty needs more than money.

fix.wrong: This tablet will alleviate from the pain.
fix.right: This tablet will alleviate the pain.
fix.why: Alleviate takes a direct object, with no preposition.

distractors: To blame someone for a problem.
tip: Alleviate reduces a problem; it does not remove it completely.

definition: To publicly support an idea, plan or cause.
examples: She advocates better pay for nurses.
Many doctors advocate drinking more water.

cloze.sentence: Our group will ___ equal education for girls.

formDrill.sentence: Years of ___ finally led to a new law.

fix.wrong: He advocates to reduce costs.
fix.right: He advocates reducing costs.
fix.why: Advocate takes -ing or a noun, not to + verb.

distractors: To argue against an idea publicly.
To forget a duty on purpose.
tip: As a noun (/ˈæd.və.kət/), an advocate is someone who supports a cause.

definition: To give something to someone for a short time, expecting it back.
examples: Could you lend me ten thousand naira until Friday?
He lent his bike to a neighbor.

pattern.rule: lend + person + thing / lend + thing + to + person
pattern.example: Lend me your book. / Lend your book to me.

cloze.sentence: Can you ___ me your phone for a minute? Mine is dead.

formDrill.sentence: The bank is the largest ___ in the country.

fix.wrong: He lended me his car.
fix.right: He lent me his car.
fix.why: The past of 'lend' is 'lent'.

distractors: To take something and keep it forever.
To ask for money in a polite way.
To sell something for less than its value.
tip: Irregular: lend, lent, lent. Don't mix it up with borrow.

definition: So interesting or convincing that you cannot ignore it.
examples: She gave a compelling talk about climate change.
There is compelling evidence that the drug works.

cloze.sentence: The lawyer presented ___ evidence that the contract was broken.

formDrill.sentence: The film tells the story ___ and keeps you watching.

fix.wrong: The film was so compelled that I watched it twice.
fix.right: The film was so compelling that I watched it twice.
fix.why: Use -ing for the thing that compels; -ed describes the person.

tip: 'Compelling' is often used for arguments, reasons and stories.

definition: Including everything important; complete and thorough.
examples: The hotel offers comprehensive insurance for all guests.
We wrote a comprehensive report on last year's sales.

cloze.sentence: Her notes are so ___ that I don't need the textbook.

formDrill.sentence: The committee ___ reviewed every claim.

fix.wrong: The instructions were not comprehensive, so I could not follow them.
fix.right: The instructions were not comprehensible, so I could not follow them.
fix.why: 'Comprehensive' means complete; 'comprehensible' means easy to understand.

distractors: Only about a small part of a subject.
tip: Comprehensive (complete) is different from comprehensible (understandable).

definition: General agreement among all or most people in a group.
examples: The team reached a consensus on the new schedule.
There is no consensus among doctors about the best treatment.

cloze.sentence: After a long discussion, the board finally reached a ___.

formDrill.sentence: Police confirmed that the relationship was entirely ___, since both adults had agreed.

fix.wrong: We reached to a consensus.
fix.right: We reached a consensus.
fix.why: We reach a consensus; no 'to' after 'reach'.

distractors: A vote won by a small number of people.
A rule made by one leader.
A long argument with no end.
tip: Spelling: con-sen-sus. It is not 'concensus'; the word 'census' is a different thing.

definition: To tell someone that something is good or that they should do it.
examples: Can you recommend a reliable mechanic?
My doctor recommended resting for a week.

cloze.sentence: I would ___ the jollof rice at this restaurant; it is excellent.

formDrill.sentence: The manager wrote me a strong letter of ___.

fix.wrong: She recommended me to try the soup.
fix.right: She recommended that I try the soup.
fix.why: Don't use recommend + person + to-infinitive.

distractors: To ask someone to join your group.
To pay someone for good work.
tip: Spelling: one c and double m: re-com-mend.

definition: Done on purpose and carefully planned, not by accident.
examples: It was a deliberate choice to keep the price low.
The delay was not an accident; it was a deliberate attempt to waste time.

cloze.sentence: Nobody believed the fire was an accident; police said it was a ___ act.

formDrill.sentence: She ___ ignored my messages to avoid the argument.

fix.wrong: He broke the window deliberate.
fix.right: He broke the window deliberately.
fix.why: Use the adverb 'deliberately' to modify a verb.

distractors: Agreed by all members of a group.
tip: As a verb /dɪˈlɪb.ər.eɪt/ it means to think carefully; the adjective ends in /-ət/.

definition: To completely remove or get rid of something that is not wanted.
examples: The company wants to eliminate waste from its factory.
Good planning can eliminate most of the stress.

cloze.sentence: Using a checklist can ___ many small mistakes.

formDrill.sentence: The ___ of unnecessary meetings saved everyone time.

fix.wrong: We must eliminate out the errors.
fix.right: We must eliminate the errors.
fix.why: Eliminate takes a direct object; do not add 'out'.

tip: Eliminate means remove completely; 'reduce' means make smaller.

definition: To make a process or action easier or help it happen.
examples: The new app facilitates payments between small shops and customers.
A good manager facilitates open discussion in meetings.

cloze.sentence: Online forms ___ the application process for students.

formDrill.sentence: The workshop ___ was friendly and kept everyone talking.

fix.wrong: She facilitated us to finish.
fix.right: She helped us finish. / She facilitated the process.
fix.why: Facilitate takes a thing (a process), not a person + to-verb.

distractors: To make a situation more difficult.
To pay for something in advance.
tip: Facilitate has a thing as its object, never a person.

definition: To say something briefly, without giving many details.
examples: She mentioned that she was changing jobs.
Did he mention the meeting time?

cloze.sentence: I forgot to ___ that the office will be closed on Monday.

formDrill.sentence: He ___ his new job only once.

fix.wrong: She mentioned about her new job.
fix.right: She mentioned her new job.
fix.why: Mention is followed directly by its object, without 'about'.

distractors: To ask for something in a rude way.
To explain something in great detail.
tip: 'Don't mention it' is a polite reply to 'thank you'.

definition: To go up and down, change often in amount or level.
examples: Fuel prices fluctuate from week to week.
His mood fluctuated throughout the day.

pattern.rule: fluctuate + between + A and B / fluctuate around + number
pattern.example: Prices fluctuate between N500 and N700.

cloze.sentence: The exchange rate can ___ a lot in a single day.

formDrill.sentence: There were wide ___ in temperature during the week.

fix.wrong: Prices fluctuate among N500 and N700.
fix.right: Prices fluctuate between N500 and N700.
fix.why: Use 'between ... and ...' with fluctuate.

tip: Fluctuate always suggests movement both up and down.

definition: To put a plan, system or decision into action.
examples: The school will implement a new attendance system in January.
They implemented our suggestions within a week.

cloze.sentence: It will take months to ___ the new payment system.

formDrill.sentence: The ___ of the plan was delayed by lack of funds.

fix.wrong: We implemented to change the schedule.
fix.right: We implemented the new schedule.
fix.why: Implement takes a noun object, not to + verb.

distractors: To stop a plan before it starts.
To write a plan on paper.
tip: As a noun, 'implement' means a tool, but this is rare.

definition: Using new and clever ideas or methods.
examples: The company launched an innovative app for farmers.
Her teaching methods are very innovative.

cloze.sentence: Our ___ design saves forty percent of the energy.

formDrill.sentence: Tech startups drive ___ in the economy.

fix.wrong: It is an innovation product.
fix.right: It is an innovative product.
fix.why: Use the adjective 'innovative' before a noun.

tip: 'Innovative' describes things; 'innovator' describes the person.

definition: To feel sad or sorry about something you did or did not do.
examples: I regret not saving more money when I was younger.
We regret to inform you that the flight is canceled.

pattern.example: I regret telling him. / We regret to inform you

cloze.sentence: She doesn't ___ leaving her old job; the new one pays better.

formDrill.sentence: It is ___ that the shop closed so early.

fix.wrong: I regret to leave school early.
fix.right: I regret leaving school early.
fix.why: Regret + -ing for past actions; regret to + verb is for bad news.

distractors: To be proud of an action.
tip: Regret + -ing = sorry about the past; regret + to = formal bad news.

definition: The quality of being honest and having strong moral principles.
examples: The judge is respected for her integrity.
Journalists must keep their integrity even under pressure.

pattern.rule: integrity (uncountable noun) + of + person / with integrity

cloze.sentence: An accountant who hides errors has no ___.

fix.wrong: She has an integrity.
fix.right: She has integrity.
fix.why: Integrity is uncountable; don't use 'an' or the plural.

distractors: Great skill at a particular job.
The ability to make people laugh.
tip: Integrity is uncountable, so no 'a' or 'an' before it.

definition: Easy to use or understand without needing to be taught.
examples: The app is intuitive; I learned it in five minutes.
She has an intuitive sense of what customers want.

pattern.rule: intuitive + noun (design, system) / it is intuitive to + verb

cloze.sentence: The new software has a very ___ layout, so training was short.

formDrill.sentence: I ___ knew the answer was wrong.

fix.wrong: The app is very intuition to use.
fix.right: The app is very intuitive to use.
fix.why: Use the adjective 'intuitive', not the noun.

distractors: Hard to learn without a teacher.
tip: Intuitive is often used for apps, websites and designs.

definition: Allowed by law or rules, or fair and reasonable.
examples: It is a legitimate business with all its licenses.
She had a legitimate reason for being late.

cloze.sentence: Make sure the website is ___ before you enter your card details.

formDrill.sentence: He ___ earned the money by running a shop.

fix.wrong: It is a legitimate reason of complaining.
fix.right: It is a legitimate reason to complain.
fix.why: A reason takes to + verb, not 'of' + -ing.

distractors: Secret and not shown to others.
tip: The opposite is 'illegitimate'; for illegal things, use 'illegal'.

definition: To succeed in reaching a goal or result through effort.
examples: She achieved her goal of running a marathon.
We hope to achieve better results this term.

cloze.sentence: With daily practice, you can ___ fluent English in a year.

formDrill.sentence: Graduating was her proudest ___.

fix.wrong: I achieved to pass the exam.
fix.right: I managed to pass the exam. / I achieved my goal of passing the exam.
fix.why: Achieve takes a noun object, not to + verb.

distractors: To try something once and stop.
To take a goal from another person.
tip: Achieve needs an object (a goal, results); use 'manage to' before a verb.

definition: Ordinary and boring, lacking excitement.
examples: He does mundane tasks like filing every morning.
She turned a mundane trip to the market into a fun adventure.

cloze.sentence: After the holiday, she returned to her ___ routine of emails and meetings.

formDrill.sentence: He explained the steps so ___ that nobody stayed interested.

fix.wrong: Mundane problems like war and climate change worry me.
fix.right: Global problems like war and climate change worry me.
fix.why: 'Mundane' means ordinary and boring, not 'worldwide'.

tip: Mundane ('ordinary') has nothing to do with 'moon' or 'monthly'.
